problem_statement: The paper frames the problem as evaluating exponential and Gaussian functions efficiently on a quantum computer, because these functions are fundamental operations and present-day general-purpose quantum function-evaluation algorithms are expensive. It also highlights first-quantized quantum computational chemistry as a motivating application where such function evaluation is needed.
problem_statement_quotes: The exponential and Gaussian functions are among the most fundamental and important operations, appearing ubiquitously throughout all areas of science, engineering, and mathematics.
Whereas formally, it is well-known that any function may in principle be realized on a quantum computer, in practice present-day algorithms tend to be very expensive.
classical_difficulty: The paper says present-day algorithms are very expensive, and that the main cost comes from quantum multiplications, which in common schoolbook form require a sequence of controlled additions and scale as O(n^2) in gate complexity. It also says the competing general-function method remains quite expensive in gates even after optimization.
classical_difficulty_quotes: Whereas formally, it is well-known that any function, f(x), may in principle be realized on a quantum computer [1–9], in practice present-day algorithms tend to be very expensive.
Each controlled addition introduces O(n) gate complexity—implying an overall quantum multiplication gate complexity that scales as O(n2).
business_stakes: The paper links the motivation to realistic NISQ applications and to quantum computational chemistry, where the ability to evaluate these functions efficiently could make first-quantized QCC more competitive. It also notes that the methods are intended to be feasible with modest qubit counts in near-term hardware.
business_stakes_quotes: Our general approach is thus equally applicable to noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) calculations [6, 20] with non-error-corrected quantum multiplications, as it is in a fault-tolerant context, using error-corrected multiplications, etc.
Space requirements are also quite modest, to the extent that the aforementioned NISQ application can be implemented with as few as ∼70 logical qubits.
extraction_notes: Motivation is explicit in abstract, introduction, and conclusion; paper is algorithmic but does state a clear quantum-chemistry application context.
